title: Notes of Ministry - 69 - August 1978

paragraphs.text: The saints should be spiritually enriched and I trust the Lord will help us to some appreciation of what spiritual riches are. I think it is the Lord’s mind for each locality that this feature should be in evidence. In what He has to say to Smyrna He speaks not only of their being rich, but of their tribulation and poverty. In the pathway of Jesus on the public side those things were very evident, tribulation and poverty, but, to the anointed eye, what riches were there!

I read from Corinthians because, firstly, in this chapter we have a reference to the assemblies, that is, local gatherings. Paul is stimulating the brethren in Corinth by referring to other local assemblies. This is a thing we should notice and follow, because if there is spiritual prosperity in local assemblies the Lord would use it for the encouragement of all. Incentives are offered in human affairs, but in the divine system the blessed Lord is extending certain incentives to us so that local assemblies may be prospered, as they were in Macedonia. We have a letter to one of them—the letter to the Philippians. At Ephesus Paul had not held back anything of what was profitable; he had not shrunk from announcing the whole counsel of God. The intensity of the light that must have shone through the vessel of testimony at Ephesus may be difficult to measure, the tremendous light

the Lord gave. But when you think of the brethren at Philippi what immediately impresses you is not the light amongst them but the spiritual state, a state of enrichment, to which Paul adds in the letter he writes to them. We have a passage in the second chapter of Philippians the like of which we have nowhere else in holy writ, concerning the same One of whom he says in writing to Corinth, “Our Lord Jesus Christ … for your sakes … being rich, became poor”. How the Philippians would be enriched as receiving that letter!

Now Paul is speaking of these Macedonian assemblies and their forwardness in the matter of communicating. Actually the communication was in material things, but what underlay that was the spiritual enrichment of the brethren in those assemblies. I believe, beloved brethren, that the Lord is looking for a state amongst us, and in measure He sees it, which will lead to the greater knowledge of God, of the wonder of divine purpose, and of this very matter of enrichment. He is looking for a state amongst us that will make way for that. There has necessarily been much conviction, correction, and instruction in righteousness. These things have been, and will be, necessary; but with them I believe the Lord is ready to communicate a deepening sense of spiritual enrichment. Now are we ready for that? Can we facilitate it in any way? “To whom God would make known”, the apostle says, “what are the riches of the glory of this mystery … which is Christ in you the hope of glory”, Colossians 1: 27. It is the riches of glory that we are concerned with, not anything material at all; that is all passing and will have to be left behind. We need to be balanced, beloved brethren, in the present time.
What will keep us balanced is the knowledge of God.

We may do well in prosperity, but not so well in adversity. Take Job—a rich man, with camels, oxen, and sheep, and his family, sons and daughters. They are not said to be wicked persons, it was just social life, and God came in and took all that away from Job. And what did he do? He worshipped “Jehovah gave, and Jehovah hath taken away; blessed be the name of Jehovah!”, Job 1: 21. Could we, beloved brethren, worship God if He took it away? The thing is to see what spiritual enrichment is. Let us set ourselves to receive what God is so ready to bestow. You are a believer; you know your sins are forgiven and you have received the Holy Spirit; you know something of what God is ready to give. Think of the inheritance amongst the sanctified; the Lord said to Paul, “that they may receive … inheritance among them that are sanctified by faith in me”, Acts 26: 18. These are elements of the enrichment of believers. In local companies, dear brethren, how can we prepare ourselves? How can we arrive at the state needed for this? I believe it is only as we imitate these brethren of whom Paul says, “they gave themselves first to the Lord”. Mr. Darby tells us in one of his letters (Vol. 3, p.297) that he was a lawyer; but feeling that, if the Son of God had loved him and had given Himself for him, he owed himself entirely to Him, he longed for complete devotedness to Him. That is the spirit that motivated these brethren in the Macedonian assemblies. They gave themselves first to the Lord.

Perhaps there is someone here who has never done that. Think about it! Begin to think about it now if you have never done so before. The Son of God loved you and gave Himself for you, and it is time now that we should give ourselves to Him; not for Him, it is not what you can do for Him; it is what He has done for you in the first place.

We love because He first loved us; but we can give ourselves to Him. The marital relationship underlies Paul’s ministry. Here it is so, and it involves what a wife does—she gives herself to her husband. When I say the marital relationship, I am speaking spiritually as to your link with Christ, and the link of the local assembly with Christ. They gave themselves first to the Lord. What affection there was for Christ in these local assemblies! They would not have to spend long deciding whether this was permissible, or that; they would not spend long deciding how much they could give to the poor saints, for they had given themselves first to the Lord. How many questions are settled in a moment when you have given yourself first to the Lord. It is not the life of a recluse, nor is it monasticism; it is not physical separation or isolation, because these brethren, having first given themselves to the Lord, gave themselves. Paul says, “to us”. How serviceable they were! How they would serve one another in love! Well, I believe that is the condition which is required in order that we might be further enriched.

In writing to the Philippians, as I have said, Paul adds to what was already there in what he discloses in chapter two. To the Corinthians he says, “Ye know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that for your sakes he, being rich, became poor”. “Subsisting in the form of God”, as he says in Philippians, and “being rich”, are allusions to His deity. He emptied Himself; that is related to His deity. He left one condition and He took upon Himself another condition.

“Being found in figure as a man” was the condition into which He came; such an One, as the footnote says (see note ‘c’, 2 Corinthians 8: 9, ‘such a one as he’), came into the condition in which we are, that is, flesh and blood, sin apart. He came into it that He might die out
of it, that He might open up for us a way, here and now, into the purpose of God. Do you not love Him for that?

I say it is time, beloved brethren, that we gave ourselves to Him. One might say, ‘How do I begin?’. That is a good question. You have a body. Paul says, “I beseech you therefore, brethren, by the compassions of God, to present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable to God, which is your intelligent service”, Romans 12: 1. The word used there for

‘service’ means priestly service. That is how you begin. That is how this change in a person’s life comes about. Let me say this, it is an irreversible change; it is a change of that kind, so that we never can be what we were; we can never go back. I do not speak lightly; I would speak in the spirit in which Peter spoke, “Lord, to whom shall we go?”, John 6: 68. That is the language of a person who has given himself first to the Lord. We may say, ‘He made many blunders’. And so have we. The Lord does not, in that sense, hold against us our blunders. He looks on the heart. He looks on the heart of every one of His own, and He looks on the heart of every local assembly. The prophet was to speak to the heart of Jerusalem (Isaiah 40: 2). Every local assembly has a heart, and the Lord speaks to it—“This is my body, which is for you”, 1 Corinthians 11: 24. It is in that language that He speaks. What an incentive to devotion, to committal!

I have read from Revelation where, again, it is a local assembly, Smyrna, to which the Lord is communicating by the pen of John the apostle, the prophet, the brother. “These things says the first and the last, who became dead, and lived”. That is how He presents Himself.
“Became dead”, a touching allusion to His becoming what He was not before; it is how He speaks to John, “I am the first and the

last, and the living one: and I became dead”, Revelation 1: 17, 18. Think of that—the Word became flesh, being found in fashion as a Man; He came into that condition in order that He might become dead. How deeply these things should affect us! Not only did the Lord come down from heaven, but from the position He had taken in having come down from heaven He descended into the lower parts of the earth in becoming obedient even unto death. He says here, “who became dead, and lived”. He not only lives, but He loves. Do you realise that?

John says, “To him who loves us”, Revelation 1: 5. He is writing in the present experience of Christ’s love. Well, He became dead and lived, so there is such a thing as life beyond death, but there may be those here who have not begun to think of that yet—life beyond death; not life on this side of death; on that side of death. “That world, and the resurrection”, the Lord says (Luke 20: 35)— that world. Do you find your affections drawn to the One who is the Centre of that world, the One who was lifted up? “I, if I be lifted up … will draw all to me”, John 12: 32. Do you find your affections being drawn to Christ, the One who was lifted up?—drawn out of the world, surely, quickly, too. Come out of it! Flee for refuge! We are among those who have fled for refuge; we are indeed. Whence have we fled? I trust that we have fled the world, yea more, we have fled from the earth. Flee from the earth to heaven!

The epistle to the Hebrews is written to incite our interest in better things. Solomon has much to say about better things in Ecclesiastes; Paul has more to say about better things in Hebrews. Solomon speaks of what is under the sun, important things. We would not set them aside for a moment. “Better is a handful with quietness, than both hands full with labour and pursuit of the wind”, Ecclesiastes 4: 6. That is one thing that Solomon speaks of as being

better. He speaks about young people, too, of youth. “Better is a poor but wise youth than an old and foolish king, who knoweth no more how to be admonished”, Ecclesiastes 4: 13. So perhaps you could come in there, under the heading of a poor and wise youth. The same book speaks of a poor and wise youth, and of a poor and wise man who delivered a city. These are the principles on which God operates, poverty of spirit, unpretentiousness, lowliness, meekness. These are the principles of God’s world. I would say again, Do you find your heart drawn to the One who is the centre of that world? Have you ever heard a voice in your own soul, speaking from the unseen world? Mr. Darby heard it, you know, in 1832. He was at that time quite a young man, with his life ahead of him as far as he knew, when he wrote—
‘What powerful, mighty Voice, so near,
Calls me from earth apart—
Reaches with tones so still, so clear,
From th’unseen world my heart?’
(J.N.D., ‘Spiritual Songs’, ‘The Call’)
So he became devoted to Christ. Why not you and I? It is the time for it. The Lord will add quickly on the line of enrichment where He has the heart devoted to Him.

Now the Lord says, “I know thy tribulation and thy poverty; but thou art rich”. I feel I need help, dear brethren, to understand what the Lord was speaking of when He said, “Thou art rich”. I think it was the way in which He was held in their affections and in their thoughts.

The value put upon Him by this local assembly involved what was truly their wealth. What a model! The persecution, the railing of those who held themselves to be Jews, He knew. He knew it, and He knows it. When He was reviled, He reviled not again; there was another order of man. “Concerning whom does the prophet say this? of himself or of some, other?”, Acts 8: 34.

Oh what a day it is when the soul gets another Man in view, the order of Man that is before God in Christ, which the Spirit of God is forming in the saints at the present time—features of the second Man out of heaven. He is the last Adam; there will be no more Adams, but many more like Him as the second Man out of heaven (1 Corinthians 15: 47). I think that in this suffering assembly that kind of man would be appreciated. Mr. Raven said, I think, that the first man is superseded. The first man was not adequate, you see, to sustain the greatness of what God had in mind for men, so he has been superseded by the second Man out of heaven. The old, man “corrupts itself according to the deceitful lusts”, Ephesians 4: 22. What has happened to him? He has been removed. This is not new, I suppose, to anyone here. It is not new doctrinally to us. But the thing, beloved brethren, is to arrive at it, not only that God removed the man that was offensive in the death of Jesus, but I am concerned to arrive at that in myself. This would enter into a way being made for the spiritual enrichment of persons, and of local assemblies.

Now in closing it is not my thought to enlarge on what the Lord says to the assembly in Laodicea, only that we should notice the contrast between the wealthy state of Smyrna, known to Christ, and the impoverished state of Laodicea, in spite of its claim to be rich. It is very important at the present time to make that distinction. “I am rich, and am grown rich”.

What a time it is in the world for that. Maybe never before has there been such opportunity on such a scale as at the present time. The natural man would say, ‘I must not miss it; it is now or never’. The Spirit of God would say in our hearts, in regard of devotion to Christ, ‘It is now or never’. Beloved brethren, how little time remains! Let us not squander time. Mr.
Taylor

remarked that it is a valuable commodity and it is in short supply. If the love of Christ does not affect us now, when will it? He loves us. Even in Laodicea there are persons He loves. He says so—“As many as I love”. Think of the Lord’s love for those who may be marked by Laodicean features. His love does not change. We may say, ‘Will not discipline come upon them?’. That question was put to a servant when someone went out of fellowship. A brother said, ‘Will he get discipline?’. The answer was, ‘Yes, when he comes back’. Such is grace!
The present moment is one of grace. If you want material things, He may say, ‘I will not prevent you’. “He gave them their request, but sent leanness into their soul”, Psalm 106: 15.

Which will you have? Ask Abraham. From a thread to a sandal-thong, he would not come under obligation to the world for a moment in regard to anything material, for he had lifted up his hand to “Jehovah, the Most High God, possessor of heavens and earth”, Genesis 14: 22.

The Lord presents Himself to Laodicea as “the beginning of the creation of God”. Think of the scope of the creation of God! Well, there it is—“Thou sayest, I am rich, and am grown rich, and have need of nothing, and knowest not that thou art the wretched and the miserable”. May the Lord keep us from it! Paul says, “Demas has forsaken me, having loved the present age”, 2 Timothy 4: 10. He just loved the present world; he loved to live on the earth. If you spoke to Lot he would tell you how to do that; you see it in Lot’s history. The greatest need is heavenly-mindedness, beloved brethren. So the superiority, morally and spiritually, of divinely-given riches is to be laid hold of by us. Esau says, “Feed me … with the … red thing there”, Genesis 25: 30. The red thing is what attracts nature. How many go after that! Esau was a man about to
die, a profane man. We are to feed upon Christ once humbled here; ‘God’s treasured store’, is to be fed upon in Christ. So that you say, ‘I want more of Christ; I desire Christ for my gain’.

The Lord grant that it may be so in all our hearts, and in our local assemblies, so that there is what He can commend and even draw attention to, as I said at the outset, “The grace of God bestowed in the assemblies of Macedonia”, mentioned to quicken the footsteps, and to awaken the desires, of the Corinthians who might perhaps have been a little inclined to dwell upon the earth.

One seeks peculiar help at this time as seeking ever to maintain the distinctiveness and glory of Jesus as to who He was, the unique character of His humanity and of His pathway here, and the uniqueness of the relationship in which He was, and is, with the Father, as it says,

“the only-begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father”, John 1: 18. One would seek to guard that in what one has to say. But I have been thinking of the reference that we read in John’s epistle that as He walked we also ought to walk. The question would be for us as to how Jesus walked. If we are to walk like Jesus, then we need to know how He walked. I believe I am right in saying that John speaks more about Jesus

walking, than any of the other gospel writers. So we can take account of John in that near place in which he was to Jesus, “the disciple whom Jesus loved”, and we can listen to him telling us how Jesus walked.

It says, “Again, on the morrow, there stood John and two of his disciples. And, looking at Jesus as he walked, he says, Behold the Lamb of God”. John the baptist had now as it were got beyond the side of his own relief. He had got through to the glory of the Person who was there. In the previous verse he says, “I have seen and borne witness that this is the Son of God”. In the earlier reference it says, “he sees Jesus coming to him”. I suppose we have all had an experience like that, each one of us having come to know the Lord Jesus as our Saviour; in that sense we have seen Jesus coming to us. He came into the world to save sinners. So John the baptist says, “the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world”

(John 1: 29). What a time it will be when Jesus is manifested; then sin will have to give way, the sin which is operating around us on every hand; but at the present time Jesus is coming to persons. He has come to each one of us who trusts in His precious blood, and believes on Him where He is in glory, having finished that great work of redemption. Each one of us is taken account of by Jesus as He comes to us, the One who has taken away our sins, having borne them in His body on the tree.

But then we come to some apprehension of the greatness and glory of the Person; come to something of the attractiveness that there was in Him as He walked. It says, “looking at Jesus as he walked, he says, Behold the Lamb of God”. Now what is the effect of it? “The two disciples heard

him speaking, and followed Jesus”. How attractive Jesus must have been, that persons who apparently had never seen Him before, as they saw Him walking felt that they must follow Him. “But Jesus having turned, and seeing them following, says to them, What seek ye? And they said to him, Rabbi (which, being interpreted, signifies, Teacher), where abidest thou?”.

There is no record in this gospel before this of anything of the preaching of Jesus; it seems to follow immediately on His baptism; yet there was something in the presence and power of this blessed, glorious Person so attractive to them that they were prepared to follow Him and to learn from Him.

What they wanted to know was where He abode. They wanted to know what His circumstances were. He simply says, “Come and see”. Oh the simplicity of it! Another has referred to ‘John’s simple page’. How profound it is, and yet what simple one—syllable words he uses! “They went therefore, and saw where he abode; and they abode with him that day. It was about the tenth hour”. How wonderful!—persons seeing Jesus as He walked, attracted to Him, prepared to learn from Him, desiring to find out where He lived, and then to stay with Him. Well, that was Jesus, in the perfection of His Person, His attractiveness, God manifest in flesh. As it says, “The Word became flesh, and dwelt among us (and we have contemplated his glory, a glory as of an only-begotten with a father), full of grace and truth”

(John 1: 14). These men would have seen something of it, and it attracted them and drew them near to Him. Where did He dwell? As that section again says, “the only-begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father” (John 1: 18). That place is His and His alone. Oh the blessedness of it! They were attracted and they saw it; “We have contemplated his glory”.

Well now, beloved, I speak guardedly and reverently in the light of the distinctiveness of the Person of Jesus, but John, who himself was a follower of Jesus, says that as He walked we also should walk. Is our walk attractive? As we are found moving among men do they see in us something which is different from other men? Do they see something which is worth following? Do they want to know the secret of it? Are they prepared to learn from us something of the secret of where we dwell? Where do we dwell? It speaks of that which is going to come upon “them that dwell upon the earth”, Revelation 3: 10. Are you dwelling upon the earth? If you are dwelling upon the earth there will be nothing attractive to men around us, because they also are dwelling on the earth. Are we persons who know something of the innermost secrets of which we have been speaking earlier, the confidants of Jesus, those to whom He would make known everything that the Father has given to Him? Are we such, and are we dwelling in relation to these things? Are we seeking the things which are above, where the Christ is? And is our walk manifesting that we are related to another scene, another order of things altogether, which stands related not to this earth, but to heaven, to the realm of the purpose of God?

Jesus walked here in all the blessed perfection and uniqueness of His own relationship with the Father. But then are we walking in the light of that in which we stand as before God, in the light of His favour? Is our walk attractive? And then, can we say, “Come and see”? Is there that being maintained here so that as we attract men by reason of what we are in our walk they can come and see? Not only that, but it says, “They abode with him that day”. O, dear brethren, I am challenged by it, as to how little there may be that is attractive in my walk. We have spoken of our dear brethren

with whom we can no longer walk. We have spoken of those around us, the many believers, thousands of them, thank God, on this island. The Lord knows those that are His, but are we walking separately, are we walking faithfully, and yet are we walking attractively, so that these persons see something which they have not got—some secret which we would fain share with them—and are so attracted by it that they would come and see, come and learn about it for themselves? And not come and see only out of, may we say, initial curiosity, but be so attracted that they would come and stay, to have their part with us in the disclosure of the mind of Christ even in this day in which we are, to know something of the place that the saints have in the purpose of God, something of the blessings we referred to earlier, “Blessed
… with every spiritual blessing in the heavenlies in Christ”, Ephesians 1: 3.

With things in the world going from bad to worse, it should be that men are looking for something which is outside of it and beyond it, something attractive. Many are weary with this sin-soiled world, weary with its pursuits and its pleasures. They should be able to see in us something which is outside it and beyond it all and be attracted to Jesus; come to see it for themselves and to be so attracted by it that they stay, not because we are there, but because He is there. They abode with Him. Oh what it is to know something of abiding with Him! It is essential in these days to know where He is and to be with Him where He is. Beloved Mr.

Raven said we ought to know where we are and why we are there. Do we know it? Do we know that we are here not only in relation to the service of God and what ministers to the heart of Christ, but we are here in relation to the continuation of the testimony? There should be a testimony to men in our walk here, that would attract them so that they might come into the

blessings which God has for them at the present time—not only the blessedness of the knowledge of their sins forgiven, but the gift of the Holy Spirit so that they might come into the light of the assembly, and might know that there is here on earth even at the present time a dwelling-place for God.

In chapter 7 it says, “After these things Jesus walked in Galilee, for he would not walk in Judaea, because the Jews sought to kill him. Now the tabernacles, the feast of the Jews, was near”. In John’s gospel the Lord Jesus is never associated with the Jewish system. The Samaritan woman in chapter 4 says, “How does thou, being a Jew, ask, to drink of me who am a Samaritan woman?”, but He leads her on to something which was beyond the Jewish system altogether. He says, “Neither in this mountain nor in Jerusalem” (John 4: 21). He leads her thoughts right away from a system to which He was never related in this gospel. So it says here that He “would not walk in Judaea”. There is that which is publicly accredited, but He is not connected with that. He is walking in Galilee. How often we have been reminded that that is the place of reproach. Are we prepared, beloved, for the place of reproach? Or do we seek a place as associated with that which outwardly professes His name, but inwardly denies Him what is due to Him?
It is significant I think that it says, “Now the tabernacles, the feast of the Jews, was near”.

The feast of tabernacles was a time when all were to be together, as it were, on one level, and it was intended that it should be a heavenly level. But now it had become “the feast of the Jews”, yet it is still referred to as “the tabernacles”. Men would have us all to be together.
Suggestions are made at times that we should sink our differences;

because we are all believers we can all be together. But it says, “the tabernacles, the feast of the Jews”. That is what it had become and it was near. These things are near to us and we know the effort of the enemy to bring things down to a common level, but if we are walking as He walked we will not be bringing things down to a common level but rather be maintaining the level which was seen in all its perfection and unique glory in Himself.

“Looking at Jesus as he walked”—Oh what a level of walk that was!—a level of things above the earth altogether, as He could say, “The Son of man who is in heaven”, John 3: 13. The level of our walk should be such, beloved, that men should be attracted into it and up to it.

We would let nothing go as to the truth; we would not compromise in any way so as to have part in “the tabernacles, the feast of the Jews”, but would be walking separately, though it may bring reproach, and be walking in such a way as to attract men into the greatest things which God has in His heart for them.

So His brethren come to Him. These things come near to us. This is the way in which the enemy would come in subtly through natural relationships that we might sink our differences and all be together on a common level, but we are not to yield in any way to such suggestions. So He says, “My time is not yet come”. They are concerned that things should be seen publicly. We hang our heads in shame as we think of things publicly, and as we think of our own part in the reproach which has been brought upon the name of Christ, even by those who have been brought into the light of the assembly and recovered to the greatest things. I believe Mr. Raven once said that if we are a witness to anything, we are a witness to the breakdown. We have had that in the
ministry, but what does it mean to us? If we have contributed to anything publicly we have contributed to the breakdown. Who can elect themselves out of it?

So it is not the time now for public manifestation. He says, “my time is not yet come”. Oh what a thing it is that His time is coming! What a time is coming! Jesus is coming! So we are seeking to be faithful to Him in the time of His rejection, walking with Him in Galilee, and breaking bread in remembrance of Himself, as the apostle says, “As often as ye shall eat this bread, and drink the cup, ye announce the death of the Lord, until he come”, 1 Corinthians 11: 26. It is the place of reproach, the place where Jesus died; but soon His time is coming, the time when He will be manifested in glory. Our privilege at the present time is to bear the reproach in view of the time when He will be manifested in glory. The world may hate us, but who can speak of the hatred of the world when we think of what Jesus suffered? He has gone before. He has marked out the path that we tread, in all its blessed heavenly attractiveness, marked out the road to Galilee.

I just refer again to Jesus walking in chapter 10. “Now the feast of the dedication was celebrating at Jerusalem, and it was winter. And Jesus walked in the temple in the porch of Solomon”. Nothing is said here in reproach as to the temple and the porch of Solomon. The days in which we live are difficult; we might say. How can we survive? How can we be true?
How can we be faithful? But wisdom is available. Jesus is “made to us wisdom from God”, 1
Corinthians 1: 30. Jesus was here walking in the temple in the porch of Solomon, so that in the place where God has been pleased to set His name there is wisdom available
to us. Think of what it says in relation to the assembly that, “We have the mind of Christ”, 1

Corinthians 2: 16. So though the day may be difficult, and though there may be problems arising which have never confronted us before (and whatever may arise we cannot go by precedent), the wisdom which comes from God, which comes from above in relation to every matter, remains and is available to us from the Lord Himself.

The Jews are concerned as to the public side, but He says, “The works which I do in my Father’s name, these bear witness concerning me—but ye do not believe, for ye are not of my sheep, as I told you”. Later He said, “He that believes on me, the works which I do shall he do also, and he shall do greater than these, because I go to the Father”, John 14: 12. How can we understand it, beloved, as we think of the works which Jesus did? But we are to think of the presence here of the Holy Spirit and of the power that there is in Him, the Spirit of Him that raised up Jesus from among the dead. Think of the power that there is for us here in our walk. We may feel weak, we may feel feeble, we may feel unable to bear the reproach, but there is wisdom and there is power available for the path. And the power and the wisdom in which we are to walk is to be for a testimony. The Lord says, “The works which I do in my Father’s name, these bear witness concerning me”. So there is to be a testimony in the way in which we are found here moving in the power of the Holy Spirit. We are to be like Elisha who was concerned that he might have a double portion of the spirit of the man who went up.
We have the Spirit of the Man who has gone up; the Spirit has come from our glorified Head in heaven, so that we have wisdom and power to walk here below.

Then Jesus says, “My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me”. “The Lord knows those that are his” (2 Timothy 2: 19)—we can leave that matter with Him; and then He says here, “And they shall never perish, and no one shall seize them out of my hand.

My Father who has given them to me is greater than all, and no one can seize out of the hand of my Father. I and the Father are one”. Think of this wonderful disclosure! Think of the security of it, beloved, so that we can walk here faithfully, cost what it may. We come back to it that we are to walk even as He walked. John is following no other and those to whom he writes are to be the same. So that if he says, “As he walked” we would understand that it could be no other than Jesus Himself, even though he does not mention Him by name.

Well, beloved, as I said at the beginning, I feel the need of great care in handling these scriptures because they speak of the walk of Jesus when He was here, in all the glory and uniqueness of His humanity, the Word become flesh. But nevertheless the fact remains that the scripture says that as He walked we also ought to walk. So are you and I walking attractively so that men enquire, and are prepared to come and see? They may wonder why we are prepared to bear reproach, but are they prepared to come and see? May we be walking even as He walked, and may there thus be a testimony to Him as we are here in power and governed by divine wisdom in these difficult days. May the Lord help us, beloved, for His name’s sake.
“It is finished”—John 19: 30
Nothing to pay? No, not a whit!
Nothing to do? No, not a bit!
All that was needed to do or to pay
Jesus has done in His own blessed way.
Nothing to do? No, not a stroke—
Gone is the captor, gone is the yoke;
Jesus at Calvary sever’d the chain
None can imprison His freedom again.
Nothing to fear? No, not a jot;
Nothing unclean? No, not a spot;
Christ is my peace, and I’ve nothing at stake,
Satan can harass, but he cannot take.
Nothing to settle? All has been paid;
Nothing of anger? Peace has been made;
Jesus alone is the sinner’s resource,
Peace He has made by the blood of His cross.
What about judgment? Now I can say
Jesus has met it, borne it away;
He drank it all when He hung on the tree,
Leaving a cup full of blessing for me.
What about terror? It has no place
Now in a heart that is filled with His grace;
My peace is divine, it ne’er can alloy;
Such is the heaven I soon shall enjoy.
Nothing of guilt? Oh no, not a stain;
How could His blood allow aught to remain?
My conscience is purged, and my spirit is free;
Precious that blood is to God—and to me!
What of the law? Ah, there I rejoice,
Christ answered its claims and silenced its voice;
The curse He has borne, the work is all done;
Law cannot condemn now a justified one.
What about death? It has now no sting,
And to the christian no terror can bring.
Death has been conquered, the grave has been spoil’d, Every hope of the enemy foiled.
What about feelings? Trust not to them!
What of my standing? Who shall condemn?
God is on my side, there’s nothing more clear—
From self, sin, and Satan there’s nothing to fear!
What of my body? That I now bring
Yielded a “holy, acceptable” thing;
It is a temple wherein He abides;
For the redeeméd all good He provides.
Nothing to pay? No, thanks be to God
All now is settled, the price was the blood!—
The blood of the Victim, ransom divine
Now by the Spirit God’s own peace is mine.
What do I wait for? Jesus my Lord,
To take down the tent and to roll up the cord,
To take me Himself to those mansions above,
Proving for ever His infinite love.
Found among the papers of Miss Lydia M. Reynolds, London, 1875–1916

“ACCORDING TO ALL MY POWER” It is strengthening to reflect on the operations of divine power which enter into the service of God. The power of Christ has provided all that is required for that glorious service to be established and maintained. This is seen in type in the devotion of David—“I have prepared according to all my power for the house of my God”, 1

Chronicles 29: 2. The immense wealth of gold and silver and other metals, and the great variety of precious stones, were the product of David’s consuming devotion to “the house of my God”. So we contemplate the power of Christ operating in all its fulness to secure a dwelling place for His God, to furnish and enrich that habitation, and Himself to set on and lead the glorious order of its service—“In the midst of the assembly will I sing thy praises”, Hebrews 2: 12. Then there is the power of the Holy Spirit as we are “strengthened with power by his Spirit in the inner man”, Ephesians 3: 16.

We contemplate, and have part in, an order of things, divinely conceived, into which enters the power and resource of two divine Persons, that there might be a habitation for God, and a rich service of response worthy of Himself as made known, and eternally satisfying to Him.

FEET WASHING “If I therefore, the Lord and the Teacher, have washed your feet, ye also ought to wash one another’s feet”, John 13: 14. This gracious service of Jesus was an expression of perfect love—“having loved his own who were in the

world”, (He) “loved them to the end” (John 13: 1). What must have been His feelings as to each? What would be His thoughts as He served Peter? He knew, and valued, his fervent love; foreknew his imminent failure; knew that he would be fully restored, to serve in powerful testimony and to glorify God in his death. What would be the feelings of Jesus as to John, one so near to Him, so lovable?

Then we are to wash one another’s feet, and that, too, is to be a service of love. It might be the feet of one experienced and mature, or of one of John’s young men, energetic and committed, or, again, of one of John’s little children, in whom the early features of the work of God are appearing. Whatever it is that we discern in one another of the work of God it is to call forth affectionate, lowly, and respectful service in refreshment and encouragement.

“The Spirit and the bride say, Come”, Revelation.22: 17. Well, who are speaking? Is every saint on earth saying, Come? I do not believe it. Some are, and what they say is accredited to all. It is the bride, the bride’s voice, and that is enough for Christ. The Spirit is speaking, and also the bride.
